fundamental.thesis: UTI AMC is one of India's older mutual fund houses, with a fee-based, asset-light model and no interest-bearing debt (net cash of about ₹273 cr). It earns mainly on equity AUM and flows, and also has pension, alternatives and international arms. H1FY27 revenue grew only 1.8% YoY to ₹983 cr, while PAT rose 10.4% to ₹426 cr; the PAT gain is mostly margin, not top-line growth. The quarter split is weaker: Q2FY27 alone works out to about ₹399 cr revenue (roughly -4.5% YoY, derived as H1 minus Q1) after Q1 grew +6.7%. The domestic business grew 3.8% while the international segment shrank 27.5%, so the 'accelerating' trajectory flag reflects lumpy treasury and other income more than a real AUM-led pickup. On valuation we did not have the AUM-linked earnings yardstick an AMC should be judged on (no AUM, flow or yield data), so we fell back to P/E and EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 30.5x, about 13% below the broad-market median and at the 42nd percentile; EV/EBITDA is 14.7x at the 25th percentile. With the stock near its 52-week low, this looks fair rather than clearly cheap for a slow-growing AMC. The biggest risk is that the company paid out 120% of profit as dividends and cash conversion was only 0.6x CFO/PAT in H1, which cannot last unless core fee growth picks up.

In Q2 FY27, net total income rose 24% to Rs 4,676 cr and PAT rose 51% to Rs 1,660 cr, with credit cost easing to 0.9% from 1.3%, ROA improving to 2.3% from 1.9%, and gross Stage 3 at 1.9%; PAT growth stayed strong at +56% in Q1 and +51% in Q2, but the table's 'decelerating revenue' and 'contracting margin' signals are unreliable because it mixes gross revenue with net income, and H1 PAT of Rs 3,460 cr also exceeds the Q1 and Q2 sum of Rs 3,288 cr. Using P/B against ROE, the lender yardstick named in the sector card rather than the 29.35x trailing P/E, the stock looks fair but full at 3.83x reported book (about 3.1x using Rs 47,778 cr equity and the Rs 1.5L cr market cap) for 12-14% ROE, at 69% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that recent profit growth leans partly on lower credit costs while capital adequacy has fallen from 20.3% to 19% to 17.3%, with next-year EPS estimates cut 1.6% and no guidance captured in the recent extracted periods.

fundamental.thesis: CONCOR is India's dominant rail container logistics PSU (~70% share in rail containerisation), operating EXIM and domestic freight corridors with an embedded structural role in India's trade infrastructure. Revenue growth decelerated to near-zero in Q1FY27 (+0.3% YoY on ₹2,160 cr) continuing a multi-quarter stagnation (Q1FY26: +2.4%, FY25: +2.7%), with PAT essentially flat at +0.1% YoY and EBITDA/PAT margins contracting to 24.5%/12.3% from their 9M FY26 peaks of 26.4%/14.4% — the Domestic segment is structurally weak at a 4.14% PBIT margin and -3.5% volume decline. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive logistics infrastructure business, CONCOR trades at 14.2× — a 39% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× (P23 percentile), with trailing P/E of 28.5× at the lower bound of the Industrials sector range (28–45×), grading as fair rather than cheap because ROE of 9.8% (below cost of equity) and a very high D/E of 7.39 undermine the P/B multiple case. The single biggest risk is management's bullish FY27 guidance (18% overall growth driven by DFC-JNPA connectivity and assured transit trains) having zero support from Q1 execution, compounded by an unquantified Land License Fee liability with Railways and a governance non-compliance flag (only 1 independent director as of June 2026), both of which create PSU-specific overhang that sell-side estimate cuts (-9.2% in 30 days, -10.5% in 90 days) are beginning to price in.

Carborundum Universal makes abrasives, ceramics and electrominerals, and has standalone operations plus overseas subsidiaries, several of which are now troubled. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 13.1% YoY to Rs 1,455 cr, easing from +17.0% in Q1 but well above the low-single-digit growth of FY26, while reported PAT fell 83.4% to Rs 12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an Rs 80.26 cr charge to wind down the German subsidiary; profit before exceptional items rose 22.1% to Rs 138 cr, led by Ceramics (+36.1%), but core Abrasives grew only 4.0% and Electrominerals profit fell 21.2%. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this business, the stock looks expensive at 34.5x, which is 47.9% above the broad-market median and at P72, and although the 115.3x trailing P/E is inflated by one-offs and the 40.1x forward P/E sits inside the 28-45x sector range, that forward multiple already assumes a sharp recovery with the stock at 85.8% of its 52-week range, ROE at 4.4%, and 4 of 6 analysts rating it a sell. The biggest risk is that the earnings recovery falls short while problems continue at the overseas subsidiaries, with Germany closing, South Africa on a non-going-concern basis and Russia's VAW on the US OFAC sanctions list; order-book data and guidance were unavailable, the peer set is a broad-market fallback, and the 38.0% dividend yield, 10.29 debt/equity and Rs 10,413 cr VAW impairment look like data errors and were not relied on.

fundamental.thesis: GPIL is an integrated steel and power producer (iron ore pellets → sponge iron → billets/wire rods with captive power) headquartered in Chhattisgarh, recently allotting industrial land at AURIC Bidkin, Maharashtra, signalling a next-phase capacity push. Revenue has deteriorated from near-flat +0.8% YoY in H1FY26 to -11.4% YoY in Q3FY26 (₹1,166 cr), while PAT margin compressed steadily from 16.3% in Q1FY26 to 12.3% in Q3FY26 — both revenue growth and margins are moving in the wrong direction over four consecutive periods. Assessed on EV/EBITDA of 13.5× (the appropriate yardstick for a capital-intensive steel business; P/E is secondary), GPIL trades at a 42% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× and sits at P22 of 473 peers — genuinely cheap, but the discount reflects real fundamental headwinds rather than neglected quality; a forward P/E of 10.9× versus trailing 19.5× implies the market is pricing in an earnings recovery that the current revenue trajectory has not yet validated. The primary threat to any recovery thesis is extreme financial leverage (D/E 7.58) paired with sustained sell-side EPS cuts (-19.1% over 90 days from only one covering analyst), which compresses the margin of safety materially if the steel-price downcycle extends into FY27.

Escorts Kubota is a mid-sized Indian tractor maker with a smaller construction equipment arm; agri machinery is about 85% of H1 revenue, so it behaves more like a farm-cycle manufacturer than an order-book Industrials name. Subtracting Q1 from H1 implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 3,243 cr, up 16.2% YoY (slowing from +28.3% in Q1), and PAT of about Rs 250 cr, a 7.7% margin against 12.0% in Q1; PAT fell about 21% against the reported Rs 318 cr, though it looks roughly flat if the prior-year land-sale gain sits in that quarter, and the reported H1 PAT drop of 62.9% mostly reflects the earlier railway business sale, with continuing PAT up only 2.2%. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardsticks because order-book measures do not fit this business, valuation looks fair rather than cheap at 16.3x EV/EBITDA and 22.6x trailing P/E: it is below the 28-45x Industrials range but inside the 18-28x Auto range that better suits a tractor maker, the P28-P30 peer ranks are against the broad market rather than close peers, and the 19.8x forward P/E rests on FY estimates already cut 11.6%. The main risk is that revenue growth is not reaching profit or cash, with agri EBIT margin down 340 bps to 9.3%, H1 operating cash flow at -Rs 107 cr on an inventory and receivables build, and management's margin recovery from Q4 dependent on stable commodity costs while crude is rising; the Rs 698 cr net cash cushions this, but the 1.31 debt/equity reading conflicts with it, and the 117% dividend yield, H1 EBITDA margin comparisons and +30.8% consensus upside also look unreliable, so none of them were relied on.

On the other side, the forward P/E of 11.9x (bottom 14% of the market) and P/B in the bottom 16% suggest the market already expects the Subansiri Lower and Parbati-II earnings ramp, so overall I grade it fair. fundamental.thesis: AWL Agri Business sells edible oils under the Fortune brand, along with packaged foods and industrial inputs such as oleochemicals, and reaches about 135 million households, but it earns thin margins typical of a commodity processor rather than a premium FMCG company. Revenue growth accelerated from +18% in Q1 to about +26% in Q2 (roughly Rs 22,202 cr, derived as H1 minus Q1), and H1 volume growth of 11% extends the improvement from 2-3% in Q2-Q3 FY26 and 7% in Q1 FY27, but Q2 PAT swung from +48% to about -2% YoY (Rs 239 cr vs Rs 245 cr), partly due to a Bangladesh minimum tax, while PAT margin fell from 1.8% to about 1.1%, so the 'expanding' margin signal in the trend table, which mixes half-year and quarterly periods, looks unreliable. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks fair, leaning cheap, at 9.0x (P8) and 20.7x trailing P/E near its 52-week low, because the broad-market peer set and 40-65x FMCG norm are poor comparisons for a 3% EBITDA-margin business, and 2.29x book for an estimated 11% ROE is not a clear bargain; the 54% dividend yield and 10.62 debt/equity look like data errors (debt/equity is probably about 0.11x), and the +55.6% consensus upside looks overstated because the implied price is below the 52-week low. The biggest risk is that growth keeps failing to reach profit, since edible oil volumes grew only 5%, EBITDA of Rs 4,100/MT sits at the low end of the Rs 4,000-4,500 guidance, and small moves in input costs can have an outsized effect on a margin this thin.

fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. The overriding risk is extreme balance sheet leverage (D/E 21.3×) combined with negative FCF (CFO/PAT −1.13× in Q2FY26) — at a 5.29% US 10Y yield and with PAT margins at 3%, any commodity cost spike or interest burden increase could rapidly destroy earnings entirely.

Anthem Biosciences is a contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) business, with CRDMO at 84% of H1 FY27 revenue and specialty ingredients at 16%, plus a net cash position of Rs 1,538 cr. H1 FY27 revenue fell 7.2% YoY to Rs 1,012 cr while PAT rose 7.2% to Rs 331 cr, but the quarters diverge: revenue fell 22.6% in Q1 and recovered about 7.8% in Q2 to about Rs 594 cr (derived from H1 less Q1), with Q2 PAT up 21.9% to Rs 211.5 cr, so growth has slowed from FY26's +15% and one rebound quarter in a lumpy business does not yet confirm a trend. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick here alongside growth delivery, the stock is expensive at 50.8x (P89 and 118% above the broad-market median, with no tight peer set available), and its 76.2x trailing P/E is also well above the 28-40x pharma range, leaving little room for error. The biggest risk is a de-rating if growth does not recover enough to justify the multiple, as 90-day EPS estimates have been trimmed (-1.4% this year, -3.6% next year) despite 8 of 8 analysts rating it a buy, and the data provided has no contract-pipeline figures to support the recovery.

fundamental.thesis: Cyient is a mid-cap engineering-services firm with three businesses: design and engineering services (DET, about 74% of revenue), electronics contract manufacturing (DLM), and a loss-making semiconductor unit, and it recently bought TAO Digital for about ₹2,156 cr. H1 FY27 revenue grew 23.4% YoY to ₹4,311 cr, but that growth is largely acquisition-driven, and PAT fell 19.7% YoY to ₹241 cr, so the PAT margin dropped from 8.6% to 5.6%. Profit has now fallen in every reported period (-24.9% in Q3FY26, -32.3% in Q1FY27, -19.7% in H1FY27), and the semiconductor unit lost ₹58 cr at a -16.5% margin. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA together, and the stock looks fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the 22–30x IT range, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x ranks P16 against the broad market, but ROE is only 7.8%. The low 11.9x forward P/E rests on analyst estimates that were cut 18% over the last 90 days, so it should not be trusted yet. The biggest risk is that semiconductor losses and integrating TAO keep eating into the steady DET profits, and the data has gaps: the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹1,498 cr conflicts with the filings, Q1FY27 shows two different growth rates, and the reported debt/equity and dividend-yield figures look like data errors.

The biggest risks are that acquisition debt and integration costs delay that recovery, with FY26 finance costs up 718% and net debt at 6.47x EBITDA on the extracted figures, while the October FSSAI-notice media report needs checking because its details are not in the data provided.

Q2FY27 net revenue rose 16.8% YoY to Rs 1,745 cr and PAT rose 66.1% to Rs 231 cr; the table's 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are unreliable because it mixes revenue before and after excise duty, but on a net basis revenue growth did slow from +24.7% in FY26 while EBITDA margin improved from 16.8% to 20.4%, with Prestige & Above volumes up 35.8%, Regular & Others down 9.7%, and total volume growth (+7.2%) trailing price/mix (+9.6%). Using P/E as the main yardstick with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the valuation is expensive: the 81.8x trailing P/E appears to use FY26 PAT and falls to about 62x on my estimate of trailing-12-month PAT (about Rs 796 cr), near the top of the sector card's 40-65x range, while forward P/E is 51.1x, EV/EBITDA is 40.3x, broad-market ranks are P82-P93 and the stock sits at 96% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that this price needs the premium growth and roughly 20% margin guidance to hold while grain costs, state policy and higher inventory (H1 CFO/PAT 0.82x) create pressure; three snapshot fields also look unreliable, as the 15% dividend yield and 20.94 debt/equity look like unit errors and the +16.1% consensus upside does not match the roughly Rs 3,690 price implied by market cap, and the October 28 earnings call transcript is not reflected here.

fundamental.thesis: Sagility is a mid-cap healthcare outsourcing company. About 90% of revenue comes from US health insurers (payers) and about 10% from hospitals and other providers. It is tagged IT here, but its demand comes from US healthcare operations, not tech spending. In Q2FY27 revenue was ₹2,032 cr, up 22.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹284 cr, up 13.3%. Growth has slowed from +35.7% (Q3FY26) to +29.1% (FY26) to +25.0% (H1) to +22.5%, and constant-currency growth is only about 12%, so roughly half the headline growth comes from the weak rupee. Reported PAT margin fell to 14.0% from 15.1% a year ago, and adjusted PAT grew only 8.1% even though adjusted EBITDA margin reached a six-quarter high of 26.3%. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA, the trailing P/E of 21.5x is below the IT sector's 22–30x range and sits at about the 24th percentile of the broad market (there are no close peers in the universe). EV/EBITDA is 11.4x, forward P/E is 15.4x, and cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x), so the stock looks cheap. The biggest risk is client concentration: the top 3 clients are 60% of revenue and the top 10 are 84%, and voluntary attrition is high at 25.7%. Losing or repricing a single large client could hurt badly. The yfinance dividend yield (44%) and debt/equity (11.5) figures look like unit errors, so I ignored them.

fundamental.thesis: HINDPETRO is a state-run oil marketing and refining company whose earnings depend mainly on the gap between crude costs and government-influenced retail fuel and LPG prices. Q2FY27 revenue was about ₹1,39,213 cr (H1 ₹2,84,339 cr minus Q1 ₹1,45,126 cr), up roughly 26% YoY from ₹1,10,323 cr, but this growth comes from higher prices rather than profit: Q2 PAT recovered to ₹3,625 cr (2.6% margin, partly helped by ₹3,960 cr of H1 LPG compensation) after a Q1 loss of ₹12,265 cr, leaving H1 at a ₹8,639 cr loss and H1 EBITDA margin at -1.9% versus about 6.7% a year earlier. Using P/E plus dividend yield and EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for OMCs, the headline 4.7x trailing P/E and 4.2x EV/EBITDA look like the cheapest in the market, but they are stale: they reflect FY26 PAT of ₹18,047 cr, while actual trailing-four-quarter PAT is only about ₹1,200 cr (roughly 70x). The 7.3x forward P/E is therefore better read as policy-priced and fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is crude above $100 with a weakening rupee: marketing losses could return while the balance sheet is already stretched, with short-term borrowings up to ₹35,933 cr, a current ratio of 0.57, negative interest coverage and an ₹18,049 cr unrecognised LPG under-recovery.

Revenue declined -14.6% YoY in Q1 FY27 (₹425 cr vs ₹498 cr), continuing a severe multi-quarter deceleration that saw -39.5% over 9MFY26 and -32.2% over H1FY26; PAT remains deeply negative at -₹32 cr (-7.4% margin), though marginally better than -₹64 cr a year ago — the 'PAT margin expanding' trajectory signal is misleading as it simply reflects a slightly smaller loss on a shrinking revenue base. Valuation is strikingly expensive: trailing P/E of 79.4× sits at P87 among 473 broad-market peers (+126% premium to market median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 483× is economically meaningless for a loss-making entity — the ₹25,371 cr market cap is pricing in the ₹8,280 cr ASCON Phase IV defence order optionality and GoI backing, not current earnings power. The single biggest risk is the material audit qualification — auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion citing Ind AS 115 revenue recognition failures on complex engineering contracts, inventory obsolescence, and inadequate internal controls, which means reported numbers cannot be relied upon and could be restated downward.

fundamental.thesis: RailTel is a state-owned railway telecom and IT-infrastructure company; its legacy telecom services business, which leases the railway fibre network, is now outgrown by lower-margin government project work, so the mobile-telecom sector card (ARPU, oligopoly) does not really apply. For H1 FY27, revenue grew 20.3% YoY to ₹2,039 cr from ₹1,695 cr, but PAT fell 5.5% to ₹134 cr and PAT margin compressed from 8.2% to 6.6%, continuing a slide from 8.9% in Q1 FY26 and 7.8% in 9M FY26. Revenue growth has also cooled from +33% to about +20%, and H1 PBT included ₹39 cr of exceptional items (vs ₹13 cr a year ago), so underlying profit quality is weaker than the headline. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA plus peer rank, not the card's 9-12x mobile-telecom band: 15.3x EV/EBITDA (P27 vs a broad-market median of 23.3x) and 32.6x trailing P/E (P46, near the median) grade it fair, and the forward P/E of 21.6x assumes an earnings recovery that the falling sell-side estimates (-3% over 90 days, 2 of 2 analysts at sell) do not yet support. The biggest risk is cash conversion: H1 operating cash flow was -₹42 cr and free cash flow -₹202 cr, so growth is being bought with working capital and capex rather than producing cash.

fundamental.thesis: Prestige Estates is a Bengaluru-headquartered developer with pan-India residential, commercial, retail, and hospitality assets — one of the top branded developers directly benefiting from RERA-driven consolidation away from smaller, unorganised players. FY26 full-year revenue (PDF-sourced) grew +72.7% YoY to ₹1,269 cr with PAT up +155.6% to ₹120 cr at a 9.4% margin; Q1FY27 results were filed (July 2026) but are not cleanly extracted into the trend table, and quarterly recognition is inherently lumpy (possession-linked), so the annual figure is the more reliable signal — the September 2026 CPP Investments entry into the hospitality portfolio is a strong institutional-quality imprimatur that adds further evidence of asset quality and management credibility. Per the sector card, P/E (55.2×) is structurally meaningless for developers; using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick, PRESTIGE trades at 21.6× — a 7.2% discount to the broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P46), placing it as fairly valued on the sector-appropriate metric; P/B of 4.0× with an ROE of only 8.0% is unimpressive in isolation but undervalues the embedded land bank and unrecognised backlog. The critical single risk is extreme financial leverage (D/E 105×) in a RISK_OFF macro regime with rising crude ($90.41, a direct construction-cost headwind) and a US 10Y yield at 5.29%, which together could compress developer spreads and raise refinancing costs if pre-sales momentum or collections slow.

Valuation is graded on EV/pre-sales per the sector card (P/E is explicitly not meaningful here; the trailing 10.25× is an artefact of the one-off gain and the P6 peer-cheapness rank must be disregarded on that basis): EV/FY25 bookings brackets ~1.0–1.9× depending on whether the full ₹8,750 cr IFC NCD is treated as net debt, putting the stock in a fair range relative to branded-developer peers with lower execution risk. The dominant risk is the ₹8,750 cr NCD at 11% p.a. demanding ~₹729 cr quarterly principal repayments from April 2026, against a DSCR of 0.09× and FY26 finance costs already up 17.1% YoY to ₹603 cr — any booking-velocity slowdown or possession delay materially raises refinancing risk.

Endurance Technologies makes aluminium castings, suspension, transmission and braking parts for Indian two-wheeler and passenger-vehicle makers, with about 24% of H1 revenue from Europe and a small but growing aftermarket business. H1FY27 revenue rose 31.6% YoY to Rs 9,159 cr and PAT rose 14.4% to Rs 519 cr; subtracting Q1 implies Q2 revenue growth of about +33.5% (up from +29.6%) and PAT growth of about +21% (up from +8.0%), but implied EBITDA margin fell from 13.1% to about 12.1% (H1: 12.6% vs 14.0% a year ago), and removing the Rs 36 cr pre-tax exceptional gain cuts H1 PAT growth to roughly +8%. Using P/E against the Auto range because no tight peer set was available, the stock looks expensive at 39.4x trailing versus the 18-28x benchmark; 26.4x forward is within range but relies on a sharp profit recovery while current-year EPS estimates were cut 4%, and EV/EBITDA of 18.7x gives only partial comfort because its P37 rank is against the broad market. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit if aluminium costs, new-plant ramp-up or the Fondalpress integration delay the margin recovery management expects; the snapshot also looks unreliable in places, as the 42% dividend yield and 19.39 debt/equity are probably unit errors, and the quoted +31.7% target upside looks closer to +17% at the roughly Rs 2,716 price implied by market cap.

fundamental.thesis: Indraprastha Gas is the main city gas distributor in the Delhi region, selling CNG and piped gas, and H1 FY27 volumes grew a healthy 6.9% YoY to 9.86 MMSCMD. The 'accelerating' revenue signal is misleading because it compares periods of different lengths: H1 revenue rose 21.4% to Rs 10,654 cr and PAT fell 71.1% to Rs 211 cr, as gas costs jumped 39%, EBITDA margin dropped from 12% to 3%, and Q2 alone had EBITDA of -Rs 31 cr and PAT of about Rs 26 cr, down 93% YoY. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, I grade valuation fair, not cheap: the 15.4x trailing P/E and 10.5x EV/EBITDA appear to rest on FY26 earnings, and my estimates using the last 12 months are about 23x P/E (versus 10-18x for Utilities and 8-14x for Energy) and 16x EV/EBITDA, while 12x forward P/E assumes profit recovers to about Rs 1,975 cr, above FY26's Rs 1,550 cr. fundamental.thesis: Data Patterns (India) is a vertically integrated defence electronics manufacturer serving the Indian military and select international customers across radar, electronic warfare, and communication systems — a high-quality niche with exceptional gross margins (78.9% in Q1FY27) and a debt-free balance sheet (net cash ₹466 cr). Revenue grew +16.8% YoY to ₹116 cr in Q1FY27, decelerating sharply from FY26's full-year +31% growth; PAT declined -13.5% YoY to ₹22 cr while EBITDA margins compressed 526 bps YoY to 27.0% — far below management's FY27 guidance range of 35–40% — driven by staff costs surging to 36.7% of sales and the intrinsic Q1 seasonality (Q1 typically ~12% of annual revenue). At a trailing EV/EBITDA of 65.9× against a sector median of 28–45× and a trailing P/E of 99.3× (P93 vs broad-market peers, +182% premium to median), the stock is unambiguously expensive, sits at 97% of its 52-week high, and is priced for near-flawless execution — any disappointment at these multiples historically triggers 30–50% de-ratings in industrial names. The central risk is that margin recovery to the guided 35–40% EBITDA band in H2FY27 is structurally harder given rising employee costs, acquisition integration, and an order book-to-TTM-revenue ratio of only 1.0× offering thin near-term execution visibility.

Delhivery is a large Indian logistics network across express parcels and part-truckload freight, so it does not fit the sector card's order-book model and has no close peers in the comparison set. Q2FY27 revenue was Rs 3,066 cr, up 20.0% YoY, slowing from +27.8% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 8.6% to 6.7% while PAT rose from Rs 32 cr to Rs 41 cr at a 1.3% margin; parcel volume grew 32% against parcel revenue growth of 22%, which suggests lower revenue per shipment, while freight revenue grew 23% on 14% tonnage. Using EV/EBITDA plus price/sales against growth and margin delivery, the stock grades expensive: EV/EBITDA is 111x versus a broad-market median of 23.3x (P98), price/sales is 3.27x on single-digit EBITDA margins, trailing P/E of 231x is not very meaningful at such thin profits, and forward P/E of 41.5x still sits at P84, though the 111x looks definition-dependent and overstated against reported margins. The biggest risk is that earnings fail to catch up with the valuation, with FY EPS estimates cut 13.2% in 30 days and 24.9% in 90 days while 18 of 20 analysts stay at buy, although cash of Rs 4,676 cr limits balance-sheet risk.

fundamental.thesis: TARIL is a mid-cap power transformer and rectifier manufacturer directly exposed to India's ₹9 lakh cr T&D build cycle, with execution growth of 23.7% in the most recent sector KPI read, positioned at an early stage of the structural capex upcycle. H1FY27 results (official NSE filing 2026-10-13) show revenue +32.6% YoY to ₹1,312 cr and PAT +39.0% YoY to ₹146 cr at an 11.1% PAT margin — a solid recovery vs Q1FY27's softer +8.1% standalone growth — but cash flow quality has deteriorated sharply to 0.33x CFO/PAT (from 0.84x in the prior comparable period), with ₹107 cr inventory build and net debt rising 24.7% HoH to ₹559 cr, flagging heavy working-capital absorption. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card), TARIL trades at 23.3× — exactly at the P50 peer percentile and sector median — while trailing P/E of 32.6× sits at the lower end of the 28–45× Industrials range and the stock sits at 20.1% of its 52-week range; verdict is fairly valued with modest risk/reward support from the depressed price level. The primary risk to the thesis is that sustained weak cash conversion combined with a 24.7% HoH rise in net debt leaves minimal self-funding capacity, and any slowdown in order execution or lengthening of customer payment cycles could rapidly escalate balance sheet pressure on a business already running at 1.46x net debt/EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Stainless (JSL) is India's #1 stainless steel producer and #5 globally ex-China, operating 4.2 MTPA capacity across 120+ product grades on a ~₹44,000 cr TTM revenue base, with strong structural demand from government infrastructure programmes (railways, highways, airports). Q1FY27 revenue grew +10.5% YoY to ₹11,279 cr (stable, not accelerating from FY26's +9.3%), but PAT margin has contracted from 7.4% in FY26 to 6.8% in Q1FY27 as raw material costs at ~70% of revenue compress the spread; PAT growth has decelerated sharply from +27.4% in FY26 to +7.7% YoY in Q1FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (the correct metric for capital-intensive steel, per sector card), JSL trades at 6.59× — inside the 5–8× mid-cycle cyclical range and at the 4th percentile vs 473 broad-market peers — grading CHEAP, corroborated by forward P/E (13.68×) sitting at a discount to trailing P/E (18.27×), pricing in continued earnings growth. The biggest risk to this thesis is raw material cost volatility (nickel, ferro-alloys at ~70% of revenue) combined with structural Chinese overcapacity, which could further erode the already-contracting EBITDA margin (13.1% Q1FY27 vs 13.7% peak in FY26).

Gallantt Ispat is an integrated long-steel maker with captive power and a pellet plant, and it claims about 25% share in its addressable regions; it behaves like a steel-spread business rather than an order-book Industrials name, so EBITDA per tonne matters more than the sector card's order-book metrics. Revenue growth improved from +1.6% in Q1 FY27 to +13.1% in Q2 (Rs 1,146 cr), but PAT fell 30.4% YoY to Rs 61 cr, PAT margin dropped from 10.8% to 5.3% in one quarter, EBITDA margin fell from 17.8% to 9.6%, and H1 cash conversion weakened to 0.49x CFO/PAT with FCF of Rs -188 cr. EV/EBITDA, the preferred yardstick here, is unavailable, so on P/E and P/B I grade the stock expensive: the 36.9x trailing P/E is above the 12-22x Materials range, appears to reflect FY26 PAT of about Rs 484 cr, and is closer to 44x on my estimate of trailing-twelve-month PAT (about Rs 406 cr), while P/B is 5.4x and the broad-market peer rank (P53) is a weak comparison because it has no true steel peers. The biggest risk is that the price assumes a margin recovery while costs are rising, utilisation is stuck at 70% and a Rs 3,000 cr capex plan is absorbing cash; identical Rs 1,146 cr revenue in Q1 and Q2, a volume decline implied by the EBITDA figures despite 13% revenue growth, and the 14% dividend yield also need checking against the source filings, which limits conviction.
